author: world today news
title: Hay Fever Trigger: Fertilised Grassland Linked to Increased Allergy Risk
text:
Are you one of the millions suffering from hay fever each year? A new study unveils a surprising link between nitrogen fertilizers and increased allergy risk, possibly worsening your symptoms.This article dives deep into the research, exploring the correlation between nitrogen fertilizers, increased pollen production, and how these factors could affect those susceptible to allergies.
Nitrogen Fertilizers linked to Increased Hay Fever Risk: Study New research suggests a meaningful correlation between the use of nitrogen fertilizers on grasslands and a heightened risk of hay fever, impacting public health and environmental concerns.
Published in The Lancet Planetary Health , the study reveals that fertilized grasslands can produce substantially more pollen, which is also more allergenic, than their unfertilized counterparts.
The Pollen Allergy Problem: A Growing Concern Pollen allergies, including allergic rhinitis , conjunctivitis, and asthma, are increasingly prevalent worldwide. These conditions not onyl diminish the quality of life for those affected but also impose a considerable economic burden due to healthcare costs and reduced productivity.
Scientists have long suspected that atmospheric nitrogen pollutants play a role in exacerbating pollen allergies by affecting pollen composition and allergen release.However, the specific impact of nitrogen fertilizers, a major source of environmental pollution, has remained largely unexplored until now.
The study highlights that pollen allergy is a growing public health concern, causing reduced quality of life and substantial economic burden.
Key Findings: Fertilized Grasslands and Pollen Production Researchers conducted a comparative analysis of pollen samples collected from 25 nitrogen-fertilized and 25 non-fertilized grasslands in Belgium .The results were striking:
Pollen count: Fertilized grasslands exhibited an average pollen count of 3.6 mg/m 2 , which is 6.2 times higher than the 0.6 mg/m 2 found in unfertilized grasslands. Allergenicity: Blood samples from 20 participants were exposed to pollen from both types of grasslands.Immune cells showed, on average, five times greater sensitivity to pollen from fertilized grasslands. The study found that fertilized grasslands had 6.2 times more pollen than unfertilized ones, and immune cells were five times more sensitive to pollen from fertilized grasslands.
Expert Perspectives: Implications and Future Research Experts emphasize the relevance of these findings, notably in regions with intensive agricultural practices and high levels of nitrogen pollution.
These findings are relevant to the UK, where nitrogen pollution remains a concern both in agricultural areas and in cities, and is already linked to other environmental and health problems, including respiratory illness, biodiversity loss, and air and water quality degradation.
Roberto Picetti, assistant professor at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine (LSHTM)
Picetti further suggests that the study supports the need for thorough environmental policies that consider both the health and ecological impacts of nitrogen pollution. by reducing nitrogen pollution, we could help protect biodiversity and lessen the severity of pollen allergies.
While the study establishes a significant correlation, the authors acknowledge the need for further research to confirm the allergy response through direct exposure of participants to pollen and subsequent monitoring of their immune responses.
The Bigger Picture: Environmental and Health Impacts The implications of this research extend beyond hay fever,touching on broader environmental and health concerns. Nitrogen pollution is already linked to:
Respiratory illnesses Biodiversity loss Air and water quality degradation The study underscores the urgency of adopting integrated strategies to address the multifaceted impacts of nitrogen pollution, encompassing biodiversity, environmental health, and human health.
In an era of ever-increasing nitrogen pollution worldwide, particularly in regions with intensive agricultural practices, our findings highlight the urgent need for integrated strategies to not only address its biodiversity and environmental impact but also the human health impact posed by nitrogen pollution.
A Novel Approach to Pollen Assessment Other experts in the field recognize the innovative methodology employed in the study.
The results of the study arguably support the importance of species-specific grass pollen monitoring given that a subset of grass species may have a disproportionate influence on respiratory health responses during peak grass pollen concentrations.
Roy Neilson, soil ecologist at The james Hutton Institute
Neilson also raises questions about how a nitrogen-driven increase in pollen will interact with the predicted increase in pollen season severity due to climate change, suggesting a complex interplay of factors.
This research highlights the critical need for re-evaluating agricultural practices and implementing policies that mitigate nitrogen pollution to safeguard both environmental and public health. Further studies are essential to fully understand the long-term effects and develop effective mitigation strategies.
